column4: After the refusal to urge food for the poor in 69:34, this condemned person has no food except ghislin; 69:37 says who eats it, turning the source’s withheld meal into punishment.
Only sinners eat the food named in 69:36; following the failure to feed the miskīn in 69:34, it sharpens the source’s passage from withheld food to fire.
When good reaches a person, he is withholding; 70:22 immediately sets the prayerful apart, matching the source’s withholding beside its prayer word.
The God-fearing are kept away from the fire warned of in 92:14-16, a direct boundary to the source’s stingy person reaching punishment.
This person gives his wealth to purify himself, the clear reversal of the tight-fisted person in 92:8 and the source’s withheld household provision.
Pilgrims are told to eat sacrificial meat and feed the destitute poor; this joins the source’s meat and poor-food details in a concrete sharing scene.
After the sacrificial animals fall, people are told to eat and feed the contented and the needy; it turns the source’s withheld meat and hearth into a shared meal.
The condemned are told to go to what they denied; 77:30-32 describe their fire, echoing the source’s denial-to-fire sequence.
The supposed shade neither cools nor protects from flame; 77:30 introduces the shade, making a direct opposite to the source’s warming hearth.
The fire throws fortress-sized sparks; 77:31 has just denied any cooling shelter, extending the source’s shift from useful fire to punishment.
After the sparks, woe falls on the deniers, bringing together the source’s named وَيْل and fire-facing deniers.
After the passage condemns failing to urge food for the poor and devouring inheritance greedily, Hell is brought forth; this makes the source’s withheld provision and final fire one sequence.
The source begins its Hāqqah account with the left-hand book recipient wishing he had never received his record; this regret starts the same condemned person’s approach to the fire quoted in 69:31.
There is no close friend for him there; after the source’s hearth that could be shared, this gives the social emptiness of the fire-bound outcome.
The prayerful group believes in the Day of Recompense; 70:22-25 describe their prayer and share for the deprived, contrasting with the source’s heedless worship and the surah’s denier.
They fear their Lord’s punishment; 70:22-25 give their prayer and wealth-sharing, the opposite of heedlessness before the source’s fire.
They do not treat their Lord’s punishment as safe; 70:27 states their fear, contrasting with those who let the source’s warning go unheeded.
The food-givers of 76:8-9 say they fear a severe day from their Lord; their forethought contrasts with the source’s refusal to share before punishment.
God protects these givers from the evil of that day; 76:8-10 provide their food-sharing and motive, a positive boundary to the source’s fire.
They are rewarded with a garden and silk after feeding others in 76:8-9, completing the opposite outcome to the source’s withheld hearth and fire.
After feeding the orphan and needy in 90:14-16, the verse names faith, patience, and mercy; it completes the positive course opposed to the source’s withholding.
The giver has no favor to repay; 92:18 supplies his giving, contrasting with the source’s closed hand around ordinary provision.
His giving seeks only his Lord’s countenance; 92:18 states the act and 92:17 the escape from fire, completing the opposite motive and outcome.
The giver will be satisfied after the wealth-giving in 92:18 and protection in 92:17, a positive end opposite the source’s fire-bound miser.
The same passage says they greedily consume inheritance after failing to urge food for the poor in 89:18, specifying the grasping conduct beside the source’s withholding.
Their love of wealth is intense; following the refusal to urge food in 89:18-19, it explains the grasping that the source turns toward fire.
When Hell is brought forth in 89:23, the person regrets not having sent something ahead; it echoes the source’s record-to-fire sequence and its warning about withholding.

The source’s dictionary image softens a crooked stick with fire before straightening it; here God makes iron soft for David, a specific material-softening parallel, though this verse does not mention fire.
The passage sends them toward a three-branched shadow; 77:31 says it gives neither coolness nor protection from flame, making this anti-shelter relevant to the source’s hearth.
This addresses astray deniers immediately before 56:52-56 describe their judgment meal, joining denial to the source’s meal-to-fire movement.
